title: High Court bars pushback of Cooch Behar family holding Indian passports
dek: Calcutta High Court says a woman and her two children detained as suspected Bangladeshis cannot be deported unless their passports are first cancelled by due process.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Calcutta High Court has barred the West Bengal authorities from pushing a woman and her two young children across the border into Bangladesh, ruling that people holding Indian passports cannot be deported as suspected foreigners without first being given a chance to prove their citizenship.

A vacation bench of Justice Sabyasachi Bhattacharyya and Justice Arjun Ray Mukherjee, sitting during the Puja recess, ordered that the family be produced before the local magistrate within 24 hours, Millennium Post reported on Thursday. The court said the family could not be pushed back "under any circumstances at this stage", according to the Daily Times of Bangladesh (tob.news), which reported the order on Wednesday.

## What happened

According to the petition, filed by the woman's husband, a resident of Cooch Behar district, the woman and the two children were stopped by immigration officials at the Changrabandha border post in Cooch Behar on 21 October while travelling to Bangladesh on visas. They were taken to a shelter home run by Dinhata municipality, and their relatives did not know where they were until 28 October, tob.news reported. The husband's lawyer, Anindya Ghosh, told the court that all three held valid Indian passports, that the children were born in a Cooch Behar hospital and have birth certificates, and that the family had been threatened with summary deportation without any charge being filed.

The state government's counsel argued that the woman was originally a Bangladeshi national. According to the state, she admitted during questioning that she had entered India through an unfenced stretch of the border near Kuchlibari and the Dahagram-Angarpota enclave, married an Indian citizen and obtained an Indian passport fraudulently, Millennium Post reported. The state said preliminary inquiries suggested the passports and visas were not genuine. These are the state's claims and have not been tested in court.

The judges questioned that position. Justice Mukherjee asked whether forgery had actually been established, and Justice Bhattacharyya asked why no criminal case had been registered despite the family being held for about two weeks, tob.news reported. The court noted that no criminal proceedings had been started and that it had not been told of any challenge to the passports.

## What the court ordered

The bench held that deporting the family without first cancelling their passports through due process was not legally sustainable, and that the passports "must first be cancelled in accordance with the law" before any such step, Millennium Post reported. It restrained the authorities from deporting the woman and the children, and directed the state to file a detailed report on the action it had taken before the regular bench after the vacation.

The court made clear that the authorities remain free to start criminal proceedings if any law has been broken, and to cancel the passports if they are found to be fake or unlawfully obtained.

## Background

The case is one of several before the High Court over people detained in Bengal as suspected Bangladeshis. In September 2025 a division bench quashed the deportation of a group of Bengal residents to Bangladesh, saying the authorities had acted in "hot haste", and ordered their return, The Wire reported. The Centre later told the Supreme Court it would bring back some people who had been deported and verify their citizenship claims, LiveLaw reported.

The detentions are part of a wider drive. Al Jazeera reported in June that thousands of people had been rounded up across West Bengal within two weeks and either sent to detention centres or taken to the border, and that Border Guard Bangladesh said it had stopped at least 18 attempts by India's Border Security Force to push about 180 people across.

## What happens next

The family must be produced before the magistrate, where the state will have to frame any charges it intends to bring. The matter will return to the regular bench after the Puja vacation, when the state's report is due.
